text: A policy can be drafted, reviewed, approved, and published — the full Lesson 22 lifecycle — and still not have changed a single person's behavior. This lesson covers the piece that actually makes it real: enforcement.

An unenforced policy is functionally a suggestion. It's a statement of intent competing against whatever's more convenient in the moment, and convenience usually wins. Enforcement is what closes that gap between what's written down and what actually happens.

Some enforcement is organizational, not technical: training people on the rule and having them formally acknowledge it, tying a manager or owner's accountability to whether their domain actually follows it, periodic audits and spot checks, and a clear escalation path back to the governance committee.

Increasingly, governance backs policy with technical controls applied at the point data is actually touched. Role or attribute-based access control blocks unauthorized access automatically. Automated classification tags the sensitive fields a rule actually applies to. Real-time monitoring flags a violation as it happens. And an audit trail makes all of it verifiable after the fact, not just assumed.
Enforcement is what turns a document into a real rule. Next lesson covers why many of these rules exist in the first place: the regulatory landscape. See you there.
